learning_objective: 🎯 Master the flow of charge by understanding Ohm's Law, resistance, and how to solve complex electrical circuits using Kirchhoff's rules!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Current is the rate of flow of electric charge. Inside a wire, electrons don't move instantly; they slowly 'drift' against the electric field with a tiny average speed called Drift Velocity.
Ohm's Law states that current is directly proportional to voltage ($V = IR$). Resistance is the opposition to this flow, depending on the material, length, and cross-sectional area of the wire.
A cell provides the EMF (Electromotive Force) to push charges. However, the chemicals inside the cell offer their own small resistance, known as internal resistance ($r$), which causes voltage drops.

For complex circuits, Ohm's law isn't enough. KCL (Junction Rule) says total current entering a junction equals total current leaving. KVL (Loop Rule) says the sum of all voltages around a closed loop is zero.
A diamond-shaped circuit of four resistors. When the ratio of resistances on one side equals the other ($P/Q = R/S$), no current flows through the middle. It's perfectly balanced!

fun_activity.title: 🥔 The Potato Battery
fun_activity.instructions: Stick a galvanized nail (zinc) and a copper coin into a potato. Connect them to a small digital clock or LED using wires. The potato acts as an electrolyte, creating a chemical reaction that generates actual electric current!

exam_tips: 📌 Always draw the direction of loops and currents clearly when applying Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) to secure step marks.
📌 Temperature dependence of resistivity is a frequent question: Resistivity increases for conductors and decreases for semiconductors as temperature rises.
📌 In a Wheatstone bridge numerical, check if it's balanced first! If $P/Q = R/S$, you can completely ignore the galvanometer branch.
quick_recap: ⭐ Drift velocity is incredibly slow (mm/s), yet lights turn on instantly because the electric field travels near the speed of light.
⭐ Kirchhoff's Junction rule is based on conservation of charge, while the Loop rule is based on conservation of energy.
⭐ Internal resistance is the reason a battery gets warm when in use.
